Corman had finished shooting on a rented set that still had two days left on its lease, and he made the simple storefront interior set available to his brother if he wanted it. Not one to pass up a bargain, Roger Corman enlisted screenwriter Charles B. Griffith to come up with a story that could be done primarily within that single setting. Then he threw together $27,000 and, just a few days later, The Little Shop of Horrors was in the can. Even as astute a businessman as Roger Corman could not have suspected the ultimate impact his little film would have. Not only did it feature one of the first screen performances of Jack Nicholson - an actor who would go on to become one of the biggest stars of our time - the film would eventually spawn a cult following, inspire a highly-successful off-Broadway musical and finally lead to the making of a full-scale motion picture with a budget nearly a thousand times that of the original. In spite of its cheap production values and laughable script, the first Little Shop of Horrors obviously contained the seed of a very good idea. The story was fairly simple. It concerned Gravis Mushnik, the The son a te sing proprietor of a little skid row flower shop; Seymour Krelborn, his mild-mannered employee; and Audrey, the sweet and simple floral arranger who is also the secret object of Seymour's passion. Seymour's other passion - collecting and caring for exotic plants - brings 'Audrey Jr.' into their lives. Audrey Jr. is unlike any plant the world has ever seen, and public interest in the unusual flora brings prosperity to the heretofore sagging flower business. There is, however, a hitch. Audrey Jr. feeds on human blood and flesh, and Seymour finds himself caught in a never-ending search for more plant food. Despite its eventual success as a cult movie, the original film was essentially a flop, taking years to recoup even its meager investment. But writer Howard Ashman and composer Alan Menken saw in the film the potential for - of all things - a musical comedy. The result of their collaboration was an offBroadway version of Little Shop of Horrors that became a huge success. In purchasing the film rights to the stage hit, producer David Geffen was surely proposing a first in cinematic history - spending $26 million in the hope of making a good film based on a good play based on a bad film. Geffen was gambling that the success of the stage show would translate to film and that the story of a misfit horticulturalist and his man-eating plant could be an entertaining one, particularly in the right hands. Though many directors were briefly linked to the project - including Martin Scorsese, Steven Spielberg and John Landis - Geffen eventually enlisted Frank Oz to direct the film. As co-director with Jim Henson on The Dark Crystal and director of The Muppets Take Manhattan, Frank Oz seemed an ideal choice, especially since the filming would entail extensive and complicated puppeteering. Oz himself, however, did not agree. "I initially said 'no' to the project, because I just couldn't get a handle on how to do it. It wasn't exactly a comedy; it wasn't exactly a drama; and even though it had fourteen songs in it - as many as in My Fair Lady - it wasn't exactly a musical. It also had a leading character that was going to be a major special effect. With so many different elements, I just couldn't find a cohesiveness to the project in my own mind." After turning Geffen down, however, an interesting idea made him reconsider. "I hit upon the notion of making the three female street singers the film's narrators - and that became the key element that pulled the whole thing together for me, The girls allowed me, as the director, to add an overall stylishness which I felt the film needed. So I got very excited about the project and I visited David Geffen in Los Angeles. Evidently, he liked my ideas for the film because he again asked me to direct - and I agreed." Once he accepted the project, Oz was faced with all the difficulties that had made him wary of it in the first place. First and foremost was the problem of developing a style for the film since it refused to fit snugly into any one genre. "I knew the film had to be funny, but I didn't want it to be so funny that the audience didn't care about the characters. On the other hand, I didn't want the audience to care so much that they took it all too seriously. I was walking that tightrope all the time." Another possible difficulty, style-wise, was that Little Shop of Horrors in no way resembled the current vogue in film musicals epitomized by Flashdance and Footloose. In visualizing the film, Oz had to contend with its lack of trendiness. "This was an old-fashioned kind of musical, in the tradition of South Pacific and some of the others I grew up with and love. In many ways, the Muppet movies are throwbacks to those kinds of musicals - but they are basically comedies with music that is secondary, In Little Shop, the music had to be a primary consideration, and it had to be a believable part of the story. The characters break into song all of a sudden - which is not real, but if done properly can be believable. I think there is a distinction there. I don't worry about reality, but I definitely go for believability. If I had set the film in a naturalistic setting with a tough, realistic acting manner, breaking into song would have just seemed silly. You can't have Stanley Kowolski start singing. But by heightening the realism so that, in essence, the film is on tiptoes, you can make that aspect of the film believable. The camera work was heightened, the color of the costumes was heightened, the colors of the storefronts in skid row were heightened, the lighting was heightened, the delivery was faster - everything was approached to bring that material alive in an ultra-realistic way, In that environment, breaking into song doesn't seem silly at all." To realize these settings, production designer Roy Walker was brought on to the project early in the preproduction phase. "Roy was the very first person we hired, in fact. I told him that I wanted our skid row to be believable but not depressing - that I wanted it to be infused with a lot of color and a sense of fun, but I didn't want it to be Guys and Dolls. I wanted it to be very textural with all the filth and dirt, but not so much that it would drag the audience down. So Roy had to find all of those balances for me. It was a tough task - to make a musical comedy skid row that was at the same time a very believable skid row. We went through the script and I gave him my ideas and he gave me his ideas. t was a very long back-and-forth process, but Roy was just tremendous." Walker's contribution would be particularly important since the set was going to be produced entirely from scratch. Rather than going out and finding a real inner city location in which to shoot, Oz had decided from the beginning that he wanted to do the entire film as an interior stage piece. "I wanted everything to be in a very unreal situation so we could believe it - which sounds like a paradox; but I think the more real you get, the less believable it is when you are dealing with a musical comedy. In West Side Story, for example, they mixed exteriors with studio. If it had been shot either entirely outside or entirely inside, it would have been better." All of these creative decisions made - and a fine cast assembled - Little Shop of Horrors entered the production phase in earnest. Rick Moranis, of SCTV and Ghostbusters fame, had been signed to play Seymour - a role which would mark his on-screen singing debut. The role of Audrey went to Ellen Greene, who had been immensely popular in the stage version. Vincent Gardenia, Steve Martin, John Candy, Bill Murray and Jim Belushi made up an impressive supporting cast; and Levi Stubbs of the Four Tops was chosen as the voice of Audrey II. Pinewood Studios in England had been engaged for the filming: and in March 1985, work began on its huge 007 stage - so named because it had been built originally for The Spy Who Loved Me and used frequently since on other James Bond films. "Two sets were built on the 007 stage." Oz revealed. "Skid row took up two-thirds of it and the other third was used for the picturesque alleyway where Seymour and Audrey sing 'Suddenly, Seymour. The 007 stage is fifty-three feet high and that was what we needed - not so much its length as its height. Although there were four flower shops all together, the one on the 007 stage enabled us to shoot from the street to the inside and from the inside out to the street. Then there were two more shops on other stages which were built to handle the demands of puppeteering. The plant would be on one of the two stages. It took three days to move the plant from one place to another; so while it was being moved, we were able to shoot on the other stage. A fourth shop was on a special effects stage, built for the violent stuff at the end - vines coming up through the floor and smashing the clock and the phone. So that set was really only used for inserts." As important as the skid row setting was to the film, nothing consumed the filmmakers' thoughts as much as the plant which would play such a starring role. Not only did 'Audrey Il' have to grow from just a few inches to almost thirteen feet in height, it had to talk and sing, dial a phone, gesture with its vines, move itself across the floor - in short, the plant had to perform with as much range as the live actors. Finding a person to realize this horticultural wonder was of the utmost importance. "It was my responsibility as the director to talk to several people about doing the plant," Oz admitted, "but I hoped from the beginning to be working with Lyle Conway." Oz had worked with Conway several times before - on two of the Muppet movies and The Dark Crystal. "I know Lyle very well and there isn't anybody better. He has exquisite sensitivity and a great sense of humor. But, most importantly, he has an amazing range of knowledge - not only of characters, but of effects. His kind of experience is tremendously valuable when you get out there on the floor. We didn't have to go to an outside source for anything concerning the plant. We never had to say, 'Okay, Lyle can make this thing, but how do we get it to grow?' He knows about lighting and lenses and all of that stuff." Conway met with Oz and Roy Walker to decide on the overall look of the plant. Throughout the discussions, Conway tried to make sure the plant was taking a form that would complement Walker's set designs. "I felt it was important that the plant not stand out as something too different or awkward in Roy's settings," Conway commented. "Initially, Frank was favoring a cartoony sort of look - a soft kind of thing like they had in the stage show - but as time went on I think he realized that that kind of look would have been at odds with Roy's designs. My preference for the plant was more horrific, tending towards a fifties or sixties horror movie type of thing - an Invasion of the Saucer Men feeling. After a lot of discussion, Frank and I met somewhere in the middle." Breaking down the script, Conway was able to determine the number of different plants the film would require, as well as the varying characteristics of each. Although those characteristics would change dramatically as the plant grew, Conway searched for a basic look from which to start. "I went to nurseries and places like Kew Gardens in London and took a lot of pictures. I also did a lot of drawings and paintings of orchid textures and cactus stems and succulents. Once I had some ideas, I made up eight-inch maquettes in clay. I'd show them to Frank, we'd talk about them and then I'd go back and make modifications based on his input. That was how I eventually got him to agree with my vision of the plant - he was able to really see what I was talking about. Drawings or paintings are open to interpretation - everyone reads them differently. But the advantage of a maquette is that it can be photographed from many different angles. Roy made a miniature shop set in the same scale as the maquette and we put the plant in that set so we could take some photos. Eventually, agreement was reached on the visual style of the plant and Conway was able to begin actual production. The script required several versions. The first was the baby plant, potted in a coffee can, which Seymour buys from a Chinese merchant. Only about four-and-a-half inches tall in the beginning, the coffee can plant more than doubles its size once Seymour discovers the unfortunate secret of making it grow. As the plant prospers, so does Seymour; and he is soon asked prospe to bring his unusual discovery to the local radio station for an interview show. The radio station plant was one-and-a-half feet tall - still small enough to sit on Rick Moranis' lap. Though these earlier plants moved and showed definite personality, the next-stage four-and-a-half foot tall 'Feed Me' plant was the first to actually speak. Feed Me - informally named, as were its two successors, for the song it sings - requiring painstaking lipsync rehearsals and a staff of puppeteers. The next plant - 'Suppertime' - was a menacing eight feet tall. Deemed too large to adequately lip-sync an entire song, this version was also constructed in half-scale. Then, at twelve-and-a-half feet, 'Mean Green Mother' was the largest and most ominous version of the plant. Though it would not make its screen appearance until halfway through the movie, Conway decided to begin by building the Feed Me plant. As the first plant required to speak and sing, Conway expected Feed Me to need several revisions before it was perfected. "On past projects I have found that after you get something built and you work with it and discover its problems, you would just love to be able to go back and build it again - but there's never time. So I tried to develop a schedule with enough time built in to do a complete prototype and then start all over again. That worked out perfectly, not only time-wise but also in providing a puppet for the puppeteers to rehearse with as early as possible. By doing that, we were able to use input from the performers as to how the puppet could be made better or lighter or whatever. Also, starting with Feed Me and then working down from that and up from that seemed less daunting than starting with the smallest plant knowing that at the end we were going to have to build a gigantic twelve-and-a-half foot Two mechanical effects specialists were brought in to construct the mechanisms for the plants. Neal Scanlan and Chris Ostwald divided the huge project, with Scanlan taking responsibility for the smaller plants and Ostwald concentrating on the Mean Green Mother. Construction on the actual form of the plant began with a limited-detail, clay sculpture produced by head modelmaker John Blakeley and model shop crew member Stuart Smith. Taking molds from the clay model, the pod's skull and basic structure were produced in Kevlar - a lighter and more durable material than the fiberglass which is traditionally used for such purposes. "We added plant textures over the basic shape," Conway explained. "I had found a picture of a cross section of a plant cell, and we used that for the surface detail. The skin itself was latex foam laid over the Kevlar skull. It was very thick - a couple of inches - and that kind of foam isn't really meant to be cast in any volume other than for prosthetic thickness. So we had to work with it for a while to get it just right. Sue Higgins headed up our foam lab and she worked out a really nice skin for the plant." Rejecting hydraulic or electronic mechanizations, Conway had determined that all the plants would be cable-controlled. "The head itself was handheld, but the puppet had twelve armatures for the main mouth and lip articulations. We tried to keep it simple. We had done a very complex cross musculature of cables for the Mad Hatter in Dream Child and it just hadn't worked. So this time we kept it to basic cables pulling plates." Even in their simplicity, however, the mechanics still took considerable experimentation. "We did all of our experimenting on Feed Me," Neal Scanlan stated. "The lip mechanisms were controlled by cables that ran up from underneath the stage, through the stem and into the head while the jaw and head itself were actually operated by the arms and body of a puppeteer. We had the whole thing on a rig which was concealed within the stem. That rig held the cables and took the weight of the plant so that the puppeteer didn't have to bear all the weight of it. It was very heavy - we had twenty to thirty cables just going up to the head alone, not to mention all the cables which were needed to control the vine movements. We tried to keep the number of cables going to the head at a minimum so we could get a performance out of it. If it had become too heavy, it would have been impossible for the operators to move it with any kind of energy." Three different prototypes of Feed Me would be introduced and completed before one was deemed satisfactory. Throughout the experimentation and construction process, a team of puppeteers had been rehearsing the lip-syncing. Brought in by Lyle Conway, the primary lip-sync puppeteering crew consisted of Mak Wilson, Robert Tygner and Sue Dacre - all of whom had worked as puppeteers for the talking chicken in Return to Oz. "We had made some attempt at lip-syncing it ourselves," Conway recalled, "sitting around the shop with the first prototype just trying to get it to make a few vowel and consonant shapes. And it was an absolute nightmare. I didn't see how we were ever going to get that thing to talk. But we called in Mak and the others, and within a week they were getting it to say, 'Feed me, Seymour' - probably because no one had told them how hard it was going to be." For the puppeteers, the most difficult part of the rehearsal phase was not so much in getting the lips to form the shapes required, but in dealing with the changes each new prototype presented. "When we first started," Mak Wilson related, "Robert Tygner and I were just working on a mockup of the plant, trying to get it to say, 'Feed me, Seymour, feed me now.' There was going to be a film test in two weeks, and at this point we were just seeing if the lips were going to work at all. We worked with that first prototype for about a month. But by the time the

rehearsal period was over, we had to deal with three different prototypes; and every time the prototype changed, there would be changes in the shape of the lips or the way the cables worked. So it was a bit like starting all over again with each new refinement. The songs kept changing, too, which was very frustrating. And new people were being added all the time. After Robert and I had been working for a few days, Sue Dacre came in to work the little extra jaw - which was just a small flap that gave that plant some additional movement. I was on the bottom lip and Robert was on the top lip and Brian Henson then joined us to manipulate the jaws themselves. That was another big adjustment, because up until then we had been working on the lip movements without the added complication of a jaw actually opening and closing. By the time we got to the last prototype, we had pretty well worked it out, although it was still very difficult. One of the recurring problems was with the 'f' shape - we couldn't get the lips pulled back far enough to make that sound. It was rather important, of course, because this was the plant that was always saying, 'Feed me!' We never really got it. "We had to find a way for the skull to support the foam so that it would form natural looking creases when it spoke, rather than creases that looked grotesque," Scanlan explained. 'When an actual person speaks, his facial skin creases and folds in ways we consider acceptable: and we had to find a way to match that with the plant. We wound up almost 'floating' the foam on the skull. It wasn't anchored down, so it was able to shift back and forth as the plant spoke without bunching up or creasing in the wrong place. Once we got that problem worked out, we had a satisfactory prototype." The finished prototype was equipped with special mechanisms to meet the specific demands of lip-syncing. "Forming the proper shapes with the lips wasn't the main problem," Scanlan commented. "That had been done before. The problem came in trying to do it with the necessary speed. You can get the speed when you're dealing with most puppet movements because you don't have to be absolutely precise. But the lipsync had to be fast and precise, and we had to come up with mechanics that would make that possible. We used a much heavier cable than we normally do, for instance. In some cases we ran a solid wire rather than a normal cable to give us very direct control. The controls underneath the stage were very large so that even moving them a little bit would move the lips quickly. Cable controls are normally almost lap-size, but these were quite big and the operator actually stood above them and worked them through long levers." As rehearsals progressed, the puppeteering team confronted not only demands of concentration, but also of sheer physical strength and endurance. 'We had one control in each hand, about a foot-and-a-half apart," Wilson explained. "Each control had four cables on it which, when worked in different combinations, gave us a variety of movement. By pushing them both forward, for instance, the lips would form an 'oo' shape. By pulling them both back, the lips would pull back toward the teeth. By pushing them together as close as we could toward our bodies, the lips formed an 'm.' The controls were quite difficult to work - and trying to get speed out of them, just because of their size, took a lot of effort." Cable controls were not used for Brian Henson's manipulation of the jaw, however, which was achieved with a more direct 'hands-on' approach. "Brian would actually stand behind the plant with his right arm in the top jaw and his left arm in the lower jaw. He was hidden by the lower half of the back leaf, while the upper half of the back leaf was behind him. So it had to be shot to make it look like the back leaf was all in one piece. For side shots, there were handles going into the plant that he could work from the side. A pole came up through the neck which was on bungee so that most of the weight was supported - you had to actually push against it to lower it. The main problem was that the weight of the head made it tilt backwards and forwards and they were constantly fighting against that. Just the size of it alone made any quick moves very difficult." Teaching their 'baby' to speak was a long and arduous process. "We figured out how to form the words by watching how we formed words. But sometimes it was a matter of what looked best for the puppet. We could do things with our lips that didn't transfer very well to the puppet, and vice versa. It was trial and error and it was a painstaking process. We went line by line, sometimes spending eight hours a day staring at monitors that were set up so we could see how we were doing. It was literally a matter of taking a word at a time and talking through it over and over again. We'd do it at half-speed, gradually building up speed as we went along, Even by the time we got to shooting, though, we rarely did more than two lines at a time. On The Dark Crystal, Conway had wanted to try undercranking the camera while shooting the mechanical creatures in order to give them extra 'snap' when the footage was projected at normal speed. On Little Shop of Horrors, he reasoned that the technique would be even more advantageous in that it would allow the lip-sync to be performed in slow-motion with much greater precision. Doing so would ease the mechanical demands on the plant and the physical demands on the puppeteers. A major disaduantage, however, was that it would require Rick Moranis - who had many dialogue scenes with the plant, and even sang a duet with it at one point - to perform in slow-motion as well. Not surprisingly, the idea met with some resistance from Frank Oz. "The slow-motion lip-sync was the hardest sell in the movie," Conway admitted. "The only way Frank would go along with it was if the plant could do everything full-speed. So there are some shots where it was done fullspeed - shots with the plant in the background were done that way - partly because it would have been just too hard on Rick to do everything slow-motion. We could have done the entire thing in real time, but shooting it this way added an element of life to it and made it more believable. We experimented with the technique on video. Using the Feed Me plant, we shot at the highest frame rate we could get by with and still get the action we wanted. We shot at 12 frames per second, 16 frames per second and at something between 16 and 24 - whatever worked. We played it back on video to get an idea of what was working best for a particular segment. Rick was absolutely great about it. Acting with the rubber stuff is difficult to begin with - adding this element to it made it even worse." The puppeteers had some doubts in the beginning about their ability to reach even an acceptable slow-motion speed with the plant, let alone full-speed shots. "From where we started," Wilson confessed, "we didn't think we would ever get faster than 12 frames per second. In the end, we surprised ourselves by getting up to 18 and even 24 frames per second. Even though it had been decided from the beginning that we would be doing the lip-sync in slow-motion, I think everyone was still hoping we'd get up to full speed: but we knew there was no way that was going to happen. It was just too physically demanding." Three months of rehearsal paid off when Feed Me finally went before the cameras. The two-week shoot went remarkably well - not only because of the extensive rehearsals, but also because Conway and Oz had seen to it that exhaustively complete storyboards were done for every sequence involving the plant. Provided by Mike Ploog, these storyboards were photographed on video and set to the appropriate music for each sequence so that every move of the plant was carefully planned out in advance. "There was really no room for improvisation," Wilson asserted. "Every once in a while we would throw in a grimace or an expression - and if Frank liked it, we would keep it. Feed Me had a bit more mobility than the others, so we'd occasionally throw in a word out of the side of his mouth. But for the most part, we had precise movements to stick to. We were so concerned with just getting it right, we couldn't be too concerned with being clever." The shoot was also made easier by the director's wealth of puppeteering experience. "A normal director would have come in and said: 'Can it do this? Can it do that?"" Frank Oz commented. "But because of my background, I knew exactly what it could and couldn't do - I've been working with that kind of thing for a long time. I knew how hard to push the performers and when to lay off, because I've been in that situation. For The Gate, however, Cook chose a different approach. "Forced perspective is essentially the process of the hanging miniature, only in reverse," Cook explained. "A hanging miniature takes something small and makes it appear to be normal size by placing it closer to the camera. In forced perspective, something that is actually normal in size - like a man in a suit - is placed farther away from the camera to make it look small. So instead of building a miniature set and magnifying it, you build a huge set and 'mini-fy' it by placing it farther away from the camera. On The Gate, we worked with a ratio of four to one; so if we wanted to make something appear to be four feet away from the camera, we had to build it oversize and place it sixteen feet away." The technique of forced perspective has been used only sparingly in recent years. In fact, the most extensive use of the process may go back as far as 1959 when Walt Disney made the classic Darby O'Gill and the Little People. Cook's desire to use the technique dates back to his childhood when he first saw the film. "Not only Darby O'Gill, but also - though I blush to admit it - 'Manners the Butler' who was a character on television commercials of the late fifties. The backyard beyond was a matte painting by Mark Whitlock based essentially on the location house used in Toronto. But in bringing the vision of escaping Hell to life, Whitlock used a rather offbeat inspiration. "Even though we were working with an already-established setting, part of it still had to be invented because what we wanted was a surreal nighttime scene. I was standing outside our shop in Los Angeles one evening and saw a sunset that had light that was very much like what I wanted to paint. So I duplicated that actual L.A. sunset - industrial haze? - thinking it would be an interesting kind of effect." The twister itself was created with cotton that was wrapped around a thirty-foot-long circular pole. "We filmed the pole using a motion control camera," Bill Taylor explained. "We dollied down the pole at a raking angle over and over again, cycling it with dissolves to make it look longer. An added pass of flying dark debris was filmed on the motion control camera. The cotton column was then double-exposed into an area of the matte painting, going up to the point where the tornado curves upward into the sky. Then we used a split and matted in a little tiny cotton column that we filmed and rotated right on a matte painting stand." Once the tornado reaches the clouds above, it starts spewing evil and darkness into the surrounding sky - an effect that required the use of a small cloud tank. "We didn't do the entire tornado with a cloud tank because controlling liquids is maybe the hardest thing in the world to do," Taylor explained. "Even with enormous cloud tanks you can shoot and shoot and sometimes the results are great and sometimes they're not. Our previous experience with tornadoes in The Wizand The Learning Tree and the dust storm in Bound for Glory convinced us that cotton was the way to go. So only for that one element did we use liquids - when you finally tilt all the way up the tornado to the sky and see the spreading cloud of filth. Lynn Ledgerwood, our key grip, set up a very shallow glass tray with a little bit of water in it. He experimented with it for days, using various combinations of chemicals including white and black paint and glue and alcohol and vodka and God knows what else until he found a combination that would spread quickly and give a nice, oozing sort of feeling. That was photographed at high-speed and combined with mattes for the rest of the shot." When Glen sees the world being destroyed beyond his window, he gathers his courage and decides to face the Demon Lord once again. He summons the mighty beast by poking out the eyeball in his palm with a shard of glass. Then, when the creature rears its ugly head back in the foyer, Glen launches a special model rocket filled with fireworks directly into the creature's chest - a shot involving some stop-motion animation by Craig Reardon and Fumi Mashimo. "That was one of the last shots done," Cook recalled. "The rocket was on a rod which was disguised by smoke that we later matted into the shot. Craig and Fumi moved the rocket one frame at a time into a rubber duplicate of the Demon Lord's chest. The rod was from behind, pushing forward until the rocket gets into him; then the rocket was gauged and the rod was switched around to the front so that the rocket could be pulled on through. It was all done in even increments. Incidentally, that shot was a conscious lift from Harryhausen's It Came from Beneath the Sea in which a torpedo was fired into the giant octopus."

Once the rocket penetrates the creature, the pyrotechnics start exploding within its chest. In an instant, the whole house seems to be erupting as the demon struggles to regain control. In a flash of blinding light, the boy is thrown free from the house - achieved with a small puppet shot bluescreen - and fireworks explode into the sky above. As Glen gets to his feet, he watches as the greenish-gray sky slowly ebbs away, replaced by a brilliant sunrise. "The sunrise shot actually involved two different matte paintings," Taylor said. "One was of a dark green murk with just slight indications of buildings in the background; and one was of the sunrise. In photographing it, we placed a mechanical device in front of the lens that wiped from one painting to the other. It started out on the painting of green murk. We did a sort of asymmetrical wipe which slowed down progressively so you got the feeling it was heading off toward the horizon. The boy was bluescreened into the corner of the whole scene. The sun itself was a separate exposure of a hole cut in a piece of metal with a strong light behind it - that was double-exposed into the shot. To give it a realistic look, we didn't hold the boy back with a matte. Instead, we let the sunlight flare over his body like it really would. Then, for the few frames where he actually crosses in front of the sun, I just put my hand in front of the lamp causing light to flare around my fingers so that it wouldn't look like the kid was a cutout." In addition to the matte paintings and the tornado, Illusion Arts was responsible for all of the optical composites in the film. Some of the most complicated involved bluescreen shots with the minions. In one of the garden shots where the minions are swarming behind Al, the mass of creatures was actually one group of fifteen repeated twice to make it appear like thirty. In another scene, the same number of minions was replicated even more. "We repeated the creatures like crazy on the banister when the Demon Lord comes rising up behind them," explained Mark Freund, who assembled all the opticals. "In that scene, all the minions are dancing and singing and we used the same guys about four times each. For the shot with the girl in the garden, we just repeated one set; but there were two layers of little guys, one on each side. It's a technique you want to use sparingly in situations where you can hide it, where there are enough things moving around and enough action going on that your eye isn't distinguishing patterns." "When you first go into an effects film, you make a long list of the things you want to do," Tibor Takacs noted in retrospect. "Then, when you look at the budget you suddenly realize that you can't do all of that, so you trim it down. Then once you get into filming you decide you really have to put certain shots back in, or you think of other things you'd like to do, and it ke tou on the starts building back up again and gets more ambitious. On The Gate, I think we were just lucky. We almost overextended ourselves. It was extremely ambitious and we didn't have time to test or reshoot anything, but it all happened to work. Due to everyone's work on the film, and to Randy Cook's effects planning and his talent, we were able to pull it all off the first time." CINEFEX 30 • 45

It seemed like risky business, mixing wiseacre comedy with the mystical adventure genre. But given the boxoffice success of the Temple of Doom-type picture and the meteoric popularity of comedian Eddie Murphy, Paramount executives decided to combine the two in a supernatural thriller involving a streetsmart social worker's efforts to free a benevolent god-child abducted by the dark forces of evil. Described by some as a contemporary sword-and-sorcery outing and by others as Beverly Hills Cop in Tibet, The Golden Child emerged at year's end to scathing reviews but decidedly brisk business. For Paramount Pictures, the risk proved eminently worth the taking. That element of risk extended also into the province of visual effects as the frenetic denouement dictated that the heretofore human villain transform bodily into a winged demon for a hands-on battle to the death with Murphy's intrepid hero. Since a free-form documentary look was desired for the sequence, the technicians at Industrial Light and Magic found themselves wagering the success of their efforts on a prototype motion control system - still being tooled during the pressured effects schedule - that could field-record camera shakes on a liveaction location and replicate them exactly on stop-motion puppets. "It was a gamble," admitted ILM general manager TARA Warren Franklin, "but the director wanted the fight scenes between Eddie Murphy and the stop-motion demon to appear hand-held. He didn't want the standard look of locked-off effects shots with no camera movement. What we came up with - in a relatively short space of time - was a reality sense that's really quite amazing." Chosen as overall effects supervisor for the film was two-time Oscar winner Ken Ralston, a veteran of all three Star Wars films, three of the four Star Trek features and a variety of other ILM projects. On The Golden Child, Ralston worked closely with director Michael Ritchie - critically acclaimed for such films as The Candidate, The Bad News Bears and Smile - and with production designer J. Michael Riva, an Oscar nominee for The Color Purple whose genre credits include The Adventures of Buckaroo Banzai and The Goonies. The script was written by Dennis Feldman, who was inspired not only by the current crop of 'quest' films, but by a familiar quote from mystery writer Raymond Chandler: "Down these mean streets a man must go who is not himself mean, who is neither tarnished nor afraid. He must be a complete man and a common man, and yet an unusual man." Assuming Chandler's thematic essence - as well as his surname - was Eddie Murphy in the role of Chandler Jarrell, a freelance social worker who specializes in tracking down missing children. Filming the demon's aerial pursuit over the highway was an arduous affair. Only a fragment of it made the release print. As Jarrell speeds down a gravel road, the creature clips a row of telephone poles, rips a hole in the car roof - an insert courtesy of Ken Ralston, who wore a monster hand - and soars off. The location plate was filmed by Stewart Barbee on Mulholland Drive in Los Angeles, bumps and all, using the Tondreau field recorder. The moves were stored on an IBM disk. Four months later, Tom St. Amand animated the demon against a blue screen. The bumps were replicated on the puppet by playing back the disk. The one shot the Tondreau system could not handle, however, showed the demon clipping the telephone poles, which were rigged on location to topple over on cue. The interaction had to be exact; so for this particular shot, Scott Farrar and Dave Hanks projected the background scene onto a curved white card and used a point-plot system devised by Craig Hosada. "The first thing we did," explained Farrar, "was rotoscope the plate through the lens of the Vistacruiser motion control camera and devise a bounce program. By projecting the footage onto the card a frame at a time, we could plot the twists and tilts of the plate. This was very hard to do with a winding road and a camera that eventually turned to the right and pointed straight up in the air. After that was done, I had to create a plot program for the demon to hit the poles. When we added the bounce program to the plot program, however, it didn't work. So we had to refine it - and refine it some more. When we shot the puppet on the go-mo, the wings didn't flap right. Tom St. Amand had to change his dive angles several times." Complicating things further was a last-minute decision to frame the shot with a car window, since the vantage point was supposed to be from the rear of Jarrell's vehicle. A window housing was bluescreened in, but ultimately the shot - which lasted 170 frames - was scissored down to forty. What survived on the screen looked more like a flyby from Rodan. The confrontation in the tunnel between Jarrell and the demon jolts the film with frenzied violent action as dust and debris blanket the scene and the earth rumbles. It was here that the Tondreau system really helped, as we wound up using debris that wasn't intended for that particular shot. Often we matte in debris. Film tests, in fact, had been done with the demon spinning on a turntable to assess the look of its wings under different lighting conditions. Ritchie gave it the green light. The 'Night on Bald Mountain' sequence from Fantasia was our inspiration to do this. It had great actions and pauses. The timings were wonderful. But when the director complained about the wings, we had to throw the shot out! He decided that he didn't want the wings to 'read' at that point and he felt that the demon appeared to be floating as it advanced toward the gate. The redo was not as nice. Numerous last-minute changes were prompted by a series of poorly received sneak previews. As reflected in the ratings cards, The Golden Child wasn't funny enough for Eddie Murphy fans and audiences felt bludgeoned by too many special effects. Consequently, Michael Ritchie had to shoot additional comedy footage and the studio ordered some ruthless edits. Pruned, for example, was an exciting shot of the demon sideswiping Jarrell and knocking him across the room. Only a fragment of it was retained as they made contact. Gone was a scene of the demon growling, "And now, Mr. Jarrelll" after he burst through the floor of the herb shop - with perfect lip-sync on the puppet. Gone also was a visceral scene of Jarrell stabbing the creature with the dagger, superbly animated by Tom St. Amand, with a stop-motion side-step harking back to the choreography of Ray Harryhausen. Gone were six cuts of the ring of fire spiraling during the tunnel battle. Some excisions were dictated by Eddie Murphy's actions, which didn't correspond well to the demon's. Others were made to tighten things up dramatically or to mask problems in continuity. Another casualty was a dramatic scene involving a melting wall. Originally, when Jarrell entered Sardo's mansion he was greeted with the startling sight of a wall running blood-red. The villain then entered the scene, snapped his fingers and all was gone. To achieve the effect, Ira Keeler scaled two sets of miniature walls and cast them in colored paraffin. Hot lights melted the wax, the camera ran at two or three frames per second, and the scene was printed in reverse. The wall sections were shot separately and merged together in optical with Eddie Murphy bluescreened in as a foreground element. When the film was given its final sneak in Sacramento, audience response was markedly improved. Paramount was satisfied that they had a hit on their hands, The technical innovations employed in The Golden Child have proven their worth to the special effects community. The Tondreau field recorder has liberated stop-motion composites from the strictures imposed upon them by randomly-moving backgrounds, and go-motion has succeeded in imparting a naturalism to animation puppets unheard of several years back. The 'locked-off shot, it seems, has gone the way of the dinosaur. But in the final analysis, a paradox occurs. Something seems to have been sacrificed in the process. What is gained in a reality sense is often lost in a theatrical sense. Once the peculiar aesthetic of stop-motion is eliminated completely, a certain magic is gone and the effect becomes stylistically wanting. For all of that labor-intensive effort, the demon in The Golden Child could have been more easily achieved with a bluescreen marionette. On the screen, in fact, the illusion resembles just that. One tends to yearn for the studied choreography of Ray Harryhausen's films, where the ballet inspires a never-ending sense of wonder despite the inertness of the compositions. Perhaps in time, ILM will take on a project less formidable and maybe more poetic, in which Tondreau-driven creatures can truly be appreciated on a level previously reserved for the good old Harryhausen events. "The Golden Child was a difficult film," Warren Franklin conceded. "When we first saw the script, it was pretty much a straightforward fantasy, But as things progressed, the whole project began to evolve - and by the time it was finished, it was quite a different movie from the one it started out to be. For us it was difficult to watch shots hit the cutting room floor or be changed around until they fit the kind of film it had become - and it was difficult to make our effects believable within that new context which was much more grounded in the real world. But one of the things that really helped was our ability to blend our shots into the main unit action sequences without being tied down to static effects setups. We've been moving in that direction for several years now - sometimes with motion control field recorders and sometimes with various point-plotting techniques - and it always provides an enhanced sense of reality. As effects people, one of our first objectives should be to give directors the freedom to design effects shots just as they would any other shot in the film - lockedoff or hand-held or anything in between. Now that we're able to tackle moving camera shots we won't be as reluctant to do it - and in some of the shows we're planning right now, like Willow and Roger Rabbit, the camera is going to be moving all the time. With the Tondreau system, we have a very sophisticated tool at our disposal. But the specific tool is not important. What is important is the idea of camera movement in effects shots - and that idea is here to stay."
